Week 8, 14 October, 2.5 hours, pen and paper. One double-sided cheat sheet, printed or handwritten. A calculator is fine. No laptop, phone, watch, or assistant.

The exam checks that you can use the basic concepts without an assistant, and that you can think about the modelling assumptions those concepts rest on.


This prep document covers [Foundations](https://vsokolov.org/courses/files/600/01-intro.html), [Estimation](https://vsokolov.org/courses/files/600/02-estimation.html), and linear and logistic regression from [Patterns](https://vsokolov.org/courses/files/600/03-patterns.html). The problems are from the [textbook](https://vsokolov.org/html/_book/) and Labs 1--7, sometimes with new numbers. Labs 5--7 are still coming; rework them on paper when they are posted. Arithmetic stays small enough for paper: a 2-by-2, a binomial with $n=4$, a $z$-score, a posterior from three products. You will not be asked to invert a matrix, run a double sum over a Poisson grid, or prove a derivative. A Judgment item may be a printed plot. Name the pattern, name the assumption that failed, and say which way a number you already computed would move.

Week 7 (testing, predictive values, expected value) is also on the midterm. That section will be added after 7 October.

Of the 40 points, 25 are Understanding and 15 are Judgment. Problems below are marked U, J, or both. Work them on paper first.


# Reading guide

The textbook is [Bayes, Artificial Intelligence, and Deep Learning](https://vsokolov.org/html/_book/) (Polson and Sokolov). Read the sections named below. The labs and this bank are how you check that the reading stuck.

You do not need every example. You need the move in the table in the next section: name the concept, write the one-line mechanism, finish the arithmetic, say what it means, and say which way it moves if an assumption changes.

Week 7 is on the exam. Those problems will be added after 7 October. The reading for it is listed now so you can start.

# 1. Probability, independence, expectation

From [Foundations](https://vsokolov.org/courses/files/600/01-intro.html) and Lab 1. Book Chapter 1.

A probability is a number you will bet at, and it has to add to one on a partition. Independence lets you multiply; that is a modelling choice, not a fact about the world. Expectation always plugs in linearly; variance does not, unless the covariance is zero.

You should be able to: write $P(\text{at least one})$ from the complement; say when the product is good enough (a clean shift) and when it is not (Sally Clark); compute $E(aX+bY)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(aX+bY)$ from means, variances, and one covariance.

## Problem 1. A clean shift (U, J)

Lab 1 Cell 6 and the hitting-streak stop, new numbers. Book: independence is the same move as Dutch Book is for additivity --- a rule you use, then judge.

A warehouse scanner misses a package with probability $0.08$. Eight packages pass in a row. Call the shift clean if none are missed.

a. Assuming misses are independent, what is $P(\text{clean shift})$?

b. Give one reason consecutive scans are not independent.

c. Why might you still use the independence model for this probability, and name one example from class where multiplying as if independent is not good enough.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. $P(\text{clean})=(0.92)^8\approx 0.513$.

b. A jam, a bad label batch, or a lighting change hits several packages in a row. One miss can also mean the next packages are rushed.

c. Independence gives a number we can compute from one rate, and for "how unusual is a clean shift?" that number is close enough. Sally Clark is the counterexample: treating two SIDS deaths as independent turns $1/850{,}000$ into $1/73{,}000{,}000$ and makes the mother look guilty.
:::
:::

## Problem 2. Dutch Book (U)

Book Chapter 1, Dutch Book and Coherence.

A racetrack analyst quotes $P(\text{Alpha})=0.50$, $P(\text{Beta})=0.35$, $P(\text{Gamma})=0.25$ for a three-horse race. Exactly one horse wins.

a. Which axiom do the quotes violate?

b. Should you buy or sell equal contracts on all three, and what is the sure profit on a $\pm 100$ stake?

c. She revises Gamma to $0.15$. Is the book now coherent under the equal-stake construction?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. The three outcomes partition the sample space, so coherence (normalisation plus additivity) requires the prices to sum to $1$. They sum to $1.10$.

b. Sell. Take $S=-100$: collect $110$ up front, pay $100$ on whichever horse wins, profit $\$10$ in every world.

c. Yes. The prices now sum to $1$, so the equal-stake gain $G=S(1-\sum P(A_i))$ is zero.
:::
:::

## Problem 3. A mix of two salespeople (U)

Lab 2 Exercise 2; in-class stop.

You split Saturday's leads: half to Tortoise, half to Hare. $P=\tfrac12 T+\tfrac12 H$ is the average per rep. $E(T)=E(H)=1.5$, $\mathrm{Var}(T)=0.25$, $\mathrm{Var}(H)=2.25$, $\mathrm{Cov}(T,H)=-0.75$.

Compute $E(P)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(P)$. Compare $\mathrm{Var}(P)$ to $\mathrm{Var}(T)$. What did the covariance do?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

$E(P)=1.5$.
$$
\mathrm{Var}(P)=\tfrac14\cdot 0.25+\tfrac14\cdot 2.25+2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\cdot(-0.75)=0.0625+0.5625-0.375=0.25.
$$
Same mean and same variance as Tortoise alone. Without the covariance you would have $0.625$, worse than Tortoise. Perfect negative correlation is what cancels Hare's noise.
:::
:::

## Problem 3B. Oil: expected payoff is not the decision (J)

Book Chapter 1, Expectation and Strategy.

An oil company can use a standard drill or a more expensive horizontal drill. Chance of a small / moderate / large find: $0.2$, $0.5$, $0.3$. Payoffs in \$millions:

| | small | moderate | large |
|--|------:|---------:|------:|
| Standard | 20 | 30 | 40 |
| Horizontal | $-20$ | 40 | 80 |

a. Expected payoff and variance for each strategy. Which maximises expected payoff?

b. If you are risk averse, which do you choose, and what assumption about "maximise $E(X)$" just failed?

c. A geological study would reveal the size of the find before you choose the drill. What is the most you should pay for that study? What did you assume about the study?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. Standard: $E=31$, $\mathrm{Var}=49$. Horizontal: $E=40$, $\mathrm{Var}=1200$. Horizontal maximises expected payoff.

b. Standard. Maximising $E(X)$ treats a sure 31 and a 40-with-a-possible-loss-of-20 as ranked only by the mean. Risk aversion is a different loss.

c. With the study you pick standard on small ($20$ beats $-20$), horizontal otherwise: $0.2\cdot 20+0.5\cdot 40+0.3\cdot 80=48$. Willing to pay $48-40=8$ million. You assumed the study is perfect, and that you will actually switch the drill once you see the result.
:::
:::

## Problem 4. True or false (U)

Book Chapter 1, True/False Variance and Expectation. Answer each in one sentence.

a. If $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0$, then $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

b. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $\mathrm{Var}(2X-Y)=2\mathrm{Var}(X)-\mathrm{Var}(Y)$.

c. $E(X+Y)=E(X)+E(Y)$ only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

d. $E(\bar X)=\mu$.

e. Correlation lies in $[0,1]$.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. False. Uncorrelated does not imply independent, except in special cases (joint Normal).

b. False. $\mathrm{Var}(2X-Y)=4\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)$ under independence.

c. False. Linearity of expectation does not need independence.

d. True.

e. False. Correlation is in $[-1,1]$.
:::
:::


# 2. Joint tables, Bayes, evidence

Lab 2 and the second half of Foundations. Book Chapter 2.

A joint table is three distributions in one grid: joint, row/column sums (marginals), and ratios (conditionals). Bayes is the same ratio with names: prior, likelihood, posterior. $P(D\mid T)$ is not $P(T\mid D)$. The prosecutor's fallacy is reporting the second and calling it the first.

You should be able to: finish a table and read $P(Y\mid X)$ and $P(X\mid Y)$ from different denominators; update a two-type prior with a binomial likelihood; turn a 2-by-2 of counts into TPR and into PPV, and say which number Alice needs after a positive.

## Problem 5. Joint table (U, J)

Book Chapter 1, Joint Distributions. Same move as Lab 2 Exercise 1.

A credit-card book of $10{,}000$ customers:

| bal \ def | 0 | 1 |
|-----------|---|---|
| 1 (low)   | 8,940 | 64 |
| 2         | 651 | 136 |
| 3 (high)  | 76 | 133 |

a. Marginal distribution of `def`.

b. Conditional distribution of `bal` given `def` $=1$.

c. Predict status for a customer with a high balance. Compare to low balance.

d. A product team wants to pitch only to `bal` $=3$ because "that is where the defaults are." Using the numbers: who does that mix up, and what would you check before restricting the book?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. $P(\mathrm{def}=0)=0.9667$, $P(\mathrm{def}=1)=0.0333$.

b. Given default: $64/333\approx 0.192$, $136/333\approx 0.408$, $133/333\approx 0.399$.

c. $P(\mathrm{def}=1\mid\mathrm{bal}=3)=133/209\approx 0.636$. $P(\mathrm{def}=1\mid\mathrm{bal}=1)=64/9004\approx 0.007$. About ninety times more likely at high balance.

d. The team is mixing $P(\mathrm{bal}\mid\mathrm{def})$ with $P(\mathrm{def}\mid\mathrm{bal})$. Most defaults are not in the high-balance cell in count terms (64 and 136 sit elsewhere); the *rate* is high at `bal` $=3$. Restricting the pitch to high balance misses current customers in bands 1 and 2 and bothers a slice that is only 64% default, not "the defaulters." Check the purpose: collections vs a wellbeing product are different losses.
:::
:::

## Problem 6. Manchester (U)

Book Chapter 2, Manchester.

Someone in a bar is supporting Manchester United. $P(\text{born within 20 miles})=1/20$. If born there, they support United with probability $7/10$; otherwise $1/10$. What is $P(\text{born there}\mid\text{supports United})$?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

$$
P(B\mid U)=\frac{(7/10)(1/20)}{(7/10)(1/20)+(1/10)(19/20)}=\frac{0.035}{0.130}\approx 0.269.
$$
Most United shirts in a typical bar were not born in Manchester.
:::
:::

## Problem 7. Tesla chip (U)

Book Chapter 2, Tesla Chip.

Thirty percent of chips from Matsushita (3% defective), 20% Philips (5%), 50% Hitachi (4%). A chip is defective. Posterior on each manufacturer?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

$P(D)=0.30\cdot 0.03+0.20\cdot 0.05+0.50\cdot 0.04=0.039$.

$P(\text{Matsushita}\mid D)=9/39$, $P(\text{Philips}\mid D)=10/39$, $P(\text{Hitachi}\mid D)=20/39$.
:::
:::

## Problem 7B. You did not need the incidence (J)

Book Chapter 2, Lung Cancer.

Women who smoke are about 13 times more likely to develop lung cancer than women who do not. In 2016, $17.9\%$ of women smoked.

a. $P(\text{smoker}\mid\text{lung cancer})$. Let $y=0.179$ be the smoking rate and $x$ the rate of lung cancer among nonsmokers. Show that $x$ cancels.

b. Most people guess a number well below $74\%$. What did they treat as the answer instead of $P(\text{smoker}\mid\text{cancer})$?

c. The $13$ is a relative risk from a population. What would make it the wrong likelihood ratio for *this* woman?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. Smokers with cancer are proportional to $13xy$, nonsmokers with cancer to $x(1-y)$. Then
$$
P(S\mid C)=\frac{13y}{13y+(1-y)}=\frac{13\cdot 0.179}{13\cdot 0.179+0.821}\approx 0.74.
$$
The absolute risk $x$ cancels. You needed the relative risk and the smoking rate, not $P(\text{cancer})$.

b. They answered $P(\text{cancer}\mid\text{smoker})$, or the smoking rate $17.9\%$, or "$13$ times more likely so it must be nearly certain." The question is the other conditional.

c. This woman is not a draw from the CDC table: age, asbestos, a family history, or a clinic that already selected for respiratory disease. Then the $13$ is someone else's likelihood ratio, and $74\%$ is not her posterior.
:::
:::

## Problem 8. The island (U, J)

Lab 2 Exercise 4; Book Chapter 2, Island Problem.

A man is arrested on an island of $1{,}001$ people. The crime-scene trait occurs in $1$ in $10{,}000$ people; it matches him. Uniform prior. $P(\text{match}\mid\text{guilty})=1$.

The prosecutor tells the jury: "The match probability is 1 in 10,000, so there is a 99.99% chance he is guilty."

a. Prior odds he is innocent.

b. Posterior odds of innocence, and $P(\text{guilty}\mid\text{match})$.

c. One sentence to the jury.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. $O(I)=1000/1=1000$.

b. Bayes factor for innocence is $10^{-4}$, so $O(I\mid E)=0.1$. Then $P(I\mid E)=0.1/1.1\approx 0.091$, so $P(G\mid E)\approx 0.91$.

c. The prosecutor reported $1-P(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})$, not $P(\text{guilty}\mid\text{match})$. Expected matches among the other 1,000 people: $0.1$. That $0.1$ is why the posterior is $0.91$, not $0.9999$, and not a conviction.
:::
:::

## Problem 8B. A match is not a conviction (J)

Book Chapter 2, Forensic Match.

$P(E\mid G)=0.90$, $P(E\mid\text{innocent})=0.02$. Prior $P(G)=1/200$.

a. Bayes factor for a match, posterior odds, and $P(G\mid E)$.

b. A second, conditionally independent eyewitness has Bayes factor $3$. Posterior probability after both?

c. Is $40\%$ enough to convict "beyond a reasonable doubt"? What assumption about the eyewitness would make the $3$ too large?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. $\mathrm{BF}=0.90/0.02=45$. Prior odds $1/199$. Posterior odds $45/199\approx 0.226$, so $P(G\mid E)=45/244\approx 0.184$.

b. $O=3\times 45/199=135/199$, $P=135/334\approx 0.404$.

c. No. A $45\times$ match and a $3\times$ witness still leave the prior in charge. If the eyewitness is more likely to pick the person who already matched (not conditionally independent given guilt), you multiplied a Bayes factor you did not have. Same machine as the island and Nakamura.
:::
:::

## Problem 9. A closer (U, J)

Lab 2 Exercise 6.

Half the bootcamp convert 70% of qualified leads, half convert 30%. First week: 3 closes out of 4. Equal priors.

a. Likelihood ratio $P(\text{3 of 4}\mid 70\%)/P(\text{3 of 4}\mid 30\%)$.

b. $P(\text{70\% closer}\mid\text{3 of 4})$.

c. One sentence to the sales manager: put them on the enterprise book, or is four leads still "too small to say"?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. The $\binom{4}{3}$ cancels: $0.7^2/0.3^2\approx 5.44$.

b. $5.44/(1+5.44)\approx 0.845$.

c. Four leads moved you from 50% to 85%. That is not "too small to say." The enterprise book is a 15% chance you just promoted the 30% closer. Say that, then decide.
:::
:::

## Problem 9B. Likelihoods you treated as known (J)

Lab 2 Exercise 7, written part. The arithmetic is in the lab; this is the assumption.

New products have high sales 8% of the time. If sales are high, a focus group is positive 70% of the time; if low, 15%. You treat those two numbers as $P(\text{Pos}\mid H)$ and $P(\text{Pos}\mid L)$, then report $P(H\mid\text{Pos})\approx 0.29$.

a. What two distinct things can go wrong when you take focus-group reactions as $P(\text{Pos}\mid H)$? Who is in the room is one class of problem; what people say versus what they do is another.

b. If the people who show up are already more enthusiastic than the market, which of $P(\text{Pos}\mid H)$ and $P(\text{Pos}\mid L)$ moves, and what happens to $P(H\mid\text{Pos})$?

c. The 8% is the number to beat. Is 29% a launch? What would you need to know about the cost of a failed launch versus a missed hit?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. The room is not the market: volunteers, staff, or a city that already likes the category. And a stated "I would buy" is not a sale. Either way you have estimated a different likelihood than the one the posterior needs.

b. Both likelihoods of a positive reaction go up if the room is more enthusiastic than the market. The likelihood ratio $P(\text{Pos}\mid H)/P(\text{Pos}\mid L)$ can rise or fall; if the low-sales group becomes almost as positive as the high-sales group, the Bayes factor shrinks and $P(H\mid\text{Pos})$ falls toward the 8% prior. The usual failure is that a positive stops distinguishing.

c. 29% is not a launch on its own. A failed launch that is costly relative to a missed hit wants a higher posterior than 29%; a cheap test with a large upside can live with 29%. The 8% is the prior, not the decision.
:::
:::

## Problem 10. Mammogram (U, J)

Lab 2 Exercise 8; Alice in lecture.

Prevalence 1%, detection rate 80%, false-positive rate 10%. In 1,000 people like Alice: 10 have cancer, 8 true positives, 99 false positives, 2 false negatives, 891 true negatives.

a. TPR, FNR, FPR, TNR from the 2-by-2.

b. $P(\text{cancer}\mid\text{positive})$.

c. A radiologist says "the test is 80% accurate." Which of your four rates is that, and why is it not the number Alice needs after a positive?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. $\mathrm{TPR}=8/10=0.8$, $\mathrm{FNR}=0.2$, $\mathrm{FPR}=99/990=0.1$, $\mathrm{TNR}=0.9$.

b. $8/(8+99)=8/107\approx 0.075$.

c. "80% accurate" is sensitivity, $P(T\mid D)$. Alice needs $P(D\mid T)\approx 7.5\%$. Most positives are the 99 false alarms from the 990 without cancer.
:::
:::

## Problem 10B. Should Nvidia use the test? (J)

Book Chapter 2, Sensitivity and Specificity.

A chip is defective with probability $0.1\%$. The test always flags a defective chip, and flags a good chip with probability $1\%$.

a. Sensitivity and specificity.

b. $P(\text{defective}\mid\text{flagged})$ and $P(\text{flagged})$.

c. Advise Nvidia whether to scrap every flagged chip. What loss did you just use, and what would flip the advice?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. Sensitivity $1$, specificity $0.99$.

Labs 3 and 4, and the last block of Foundations. Book Chapter 1, named distributions.

# 5. Linear regression

[Patterns](https://vsokolov.org/courses/files/600/03-patterns.html), through log transforms and OLS. Book Chapter 12, up to residual analysis and log-log.

The model is $E(y\mid x)=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$ (or more columns). OLS picks $\beta$ to minimise squared residuals. The slope is a rate: the change in predicted $y$ for a one-unit change in $x$. A log-log fit is the same model after a change of representation, $y=ax^b$. Dummy variables: $k$ levels need $k-1$ columns; the omitted level is the reference, and that is a choice.

$R^2$ answers a narrow question. It is not "is this model good." A residual plot is the check.

## Problem 25. Log-log as a power law (U, J)

Book Chapter 12, Log Transformations. Same move as mammal brain/body and Apple growth in lecture.

Advertising $x$ and revenue $y$ (both in \$millions) follow $y=ax^b$. Data: $(x,y)=(1,5),(2,8),(4,14),(8,25),(16,45)$.

A log-log fit gives $\log y=1.564+0.798\log x$ (natural logs).

a. Transform the power law to a linear model.

b. What are $\hat a$ and $\hat b$? Interpret $b$.

c. Predict revenue at $x=10$.

d. Why might you prefer this to OLS of $y$ on $x$ in the original scale, even if the raw $R^2$ looks fine?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. $\log y=\log a+b\log x$.

b. $\hat b=0.798$, $\hat a=e^{1.564}\approx 4.78$. A 1% increase in advertising is associated with about a 0.80% increase in revenue: diminishing returns. Doubling $x$ multiplies $y$ by $2^{0.798}\approx 1.74$, not $2$.

c. $\hat y=4.78\cdot 10^{0.798}\approx 30.0$ million.

d. The original scale is multiplicative and the residual spread usually fans with $x$. Log-log makes the mean linear and often stabilises the spread. $R^2$ on the raw scale is not comparable to $R^2$ on the log scale, and a high raw $R^2$ can hide the fan.

## Problem 27. True or false, linear regression (U)

Book Chapter 12, True/False: Linear Regression. Also Book Chapter 11, MSE vs MAE (c)--(d).

a. OLS minimises the sum of absolute residuals.

b. Adding a predictor cannot decrease $R^2$.

c. Multicollinearity biases OLS.

d. If $y_i=x_i^T\beta+\varepsilon_i$ with iid Normal errors, MLE for $\beta$ is OLS.

e. MAE is more affected by a single huge residual than MSE is.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. False. OLS is squared residuals. Absolute residuals are LAD / MAE.

b. True. In-sample $R^2$ cannot fall when you add a column. That is why it is not a model-selection criterion.

c. False. OLS stays unbiased. The variance of $\hat\beta$ blows up.

d. True. The Normal log-likelihood is $-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(y_i-x_i^T\beta)^2$ plus a constant.

e. False. MSE squares the residual; the outlier dominates MSE more than MAE.
:::

## Problem 28. From log-odds to a probability (U)

Book Chapter 13, Sigmoid. You need the function, not a derivative.

$\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$. A fitted logit is $z=-0.5+0.4x$.

a. What is $p$ at $x=0$? At $x=0$, what does $z=0$ mean when it occurs?

b. Show, in one line, that $\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)$. Why does that matter for a "no event" probability?

c. If $x$ increases by 1, what happens to the odds? To $p$? (The second answer is not a constant.)

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. $z=-0.5$, $p=\sigma(-0.5)\approx 0.378$. $z=0$ means $p=1/2$, a coin flip under the model, which here is at $x=0.5/0.4=1.25$, not at $x=0$.

b. $1-\sigma(z)=e^{-z}/(1+e^{-z})=\sigma(-z)$. $P(\text{no event})=1-p=\sigma(-z)$.

c. Odds are multiplied by $e^{0.4}\approx 1.49$. Probability follows the sigmoid, so the same $+0.4$ in log-odds moves $p$ a lot near $0.5$ and almost not at all near $0$ or $1$.
:::
:::

## Problem 30. Confusion matrix and a threshold (U, J)

Book Chapter 13, Confusion Matrix and Metrics. Same accounting as Lab 2's 1,000 mammograms, now with a cost.

| | Predicted fraud | Predicted legit |
|--|--|--|
| Actual fraud | 85 | 15 |
| Actual legit | 50 | 4,850 |

a. Accuracy, precision, recall.

b. Why is accuracy a poor metric here?

c. Missing a fraud costs $\$500$; a false alarm costs $\$10$. Which error should the threshold lean toward, and which way do you move it from $0.5$?

## Problem 30B. What the coefficient assumed (J)

A logistic default model on last year's book:
$$
\log\frac{p}{1-p}=-3.0+0.02\,\mathrm{balance}-0.8\,\mathrm{student}.
$$
`student` $=1$ if the borrower is a student.

a. Holding balance fixed, what did the model assume the $-0.8$ is?

b. Students have higher balances on average. If you drop `balance` and refit with `student` alone, which way does the student coefficient typically move, and what assumption just failed?

c. A 0.5 threshold on $p$ is used to deny credit. What loss did that assume, and who is hurt if false denials are costlier than missed defaults?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

a. It assumed that, at the same balance, students have lower log-odds of default than non-students. That is a ceteris-paribus association in this book, not "being a student causes lower default."

b. The student coefficient typically rises (becomes less negative, or positive). Students look riskier in the margin because they carry more balance. The assumption that failed is "the other variables in the linear predictor hold the comparison fixed." Omitting the confounder changes the meaning of $\beta$.

c. Equal cost of false deny and missed default. If false denials are costlier, raise the threshold (deny only at higher $p$). Students with high balances are the group the omitted-variable version would punish.
:::
:::

# How to sit the exam

Every scored item is a concept plus a use. Write the name of the move, then the arithmetic, then one sentence in the setting of the question. If the condition named in the prompt changes, say which way the number moves.

Assumption items are the Judgment points. Use the four sentences from the front: name it, why it was used, what would make it false here, which way the number moves or whether it is still good enough. Independence is allowed when the order of magnitude is the point (a clean shift) and not when the product is the conviction (Sally Clark). iid is allowed when tomorrow looks like these minutes, and not when a flash sale sat in the sample. A 0.5 threshold is allowed when the two errors cost the same. A residual plot, a histogram against a Normal, or observed counts against a Poisson is the same four sentences, starting from what you can see.

You will not be asked to invert $X^TX$, expand a Poisson double sum, or quote a library function. If a calculation needs $\Phi$, a four-point table on the cheat sheet is enough.
